Connection Title: Hypothalamic hormones that stimulate anterior pituitary secretion
Explanation: TRH stimulates TSH secretion; GnRH stimulates LH and FSH; CRH stimulates ACTH; GHRH stimulates GH. These are hypothalamic releasing signals.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hypothalamic releasing hormones; Anterior pituitary stimulators
Source Section: Hypothalamus: Function, p. 7; Anterior Pituitary: Function, p. 16
Notes: Verified stimulatory (releasing) hormones; dopamine and somatostatin are the inhibitory counterparts and are correct distractors. Ref: Molina PE, Endocrine Physiology 5e (McGraw Hill); Van Uytfanghe K et al., Thyroid 2023.

Connection Title: Anterior pituitary hormones targeting other endocrine glands
Explanation: TSH acts on the thyroid, ACTH on the adrenal cortex, and FSH and LH on gonadal endocrine function.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Tropic anterior pituitary hormones; Pituitary gland-to-gland signals
Notes: Tropic hormones acting on downstream endocrine glands; GH and prolactin are correct non-tropic distractors. ACTH is a peptide, so a 'glycoprotein hormones' label would wrongly exclude it. Board overlap: avoid pairing with a separate glycoprotein-hormone (TSH/FSH/LH/hCG) set. Ref: Molina PE, Endocrine Physiology 5e.

Connection Title: Triggers of inappropriate ADH secretion
Explanation: Small cell lung carcinoma can produce ectopic ADH; the three medication entries are listed as drug causes of SIADH.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Causes of SIADH; Causes of inappropriate antidiuresis
Notes: All four are recognized SIADH causes (ectopic ADH from SCLC; drug-induced by SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide); 'can cause' wording accurate. SSRIs is a class while the others are single agents (acceptable). Ref: Adrogue HJ, Madias NE. SIADH. NEJM 2023.

Connection Title: Acquired causes of central diabetes insipidus
Explanation: These processes can injure the hypothalamic-neurohypophyseal system and reduce effective ADH secretion, producing central diabetes insipidus.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Causes of ADH deficiency; Causes of central DI
Notes: TBI, SAH, meningitis, and Langerhans cell histiocytosis are established acquired causes of central DI; not inevitable. Ref: Refardt J et al. Clin Endocrinol 2019; Driano JE et al. Pediatrics 2021 (DI vs SIADH).

Connection Title: Dopamine-blocking drugs that can elevate prolactin
Explanation: Dopamine normally suppresses lactotroph secretion. Blocking dopamine receptors can remove that inhibition and cause hyperprolactinemia.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: D2 antagonists causing hyperprolactinemia; Drug-induced prolactin elevation
Notes: Risperidone, haloperidol, fluphenazine (antipsychotic D2 antagonists) and metoclopramide (prokinetic D2 antagonist) cause hyperprolactinemia by disinhibition; metoclopramide prevents an 'all-antipsychotic' reading. Ref: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology 15e.

Connection Title: Structural causes of hypopituitarism
Explanation: Postpartum ischemic injury, pituitary compression, hemorrhage or infarction, and a compressive suprasellar tumor can each impair pituitary function.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Causes of pituitary hormone deficiency; Structural pituitary dysfunction
Notes: Sheehan, apoplexy, craniopharyngioma, and empty sella can each cause hypopituitarism; empty sella is often incidental with normal function, so 'can cause' wording is required. Ref: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 14e.

Connection Title: Morphologic clues to acromegaly
Explanation: GH excess after epiphyseal closure produces disproportionate skeletal and soft-tissue growth, including these changes.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Acromegaly physical findings; Adult GH excess
Notes: Frontal bossing, prognathic mandibular enlargement, interdental spacing, and acral enlargement are classic post-epiphyseal GH excess; the broader GH-excess label is acceptable only if adult presentation is preserved (vs gigantism). Ref: Katznelson L et al. Acromegaly, Endocrine Society Guideline, JCEM 2014.

Connection Title: Interventions used to treat acromegaly
Explanation: Removing the adenoma, suppressing GH with a somatostatin analogue or dopamine agonist, and blocking the GH receptor are treatment approaches listed for acromegaly.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Acromegaly therapies; Treatments for GH excess
Notes: Transsphenoidal resection (first-line), somatostatin analogue (octreotide), GH-receptor antagonist (pegvisomant), and dopamine agonist (cabergoline, adjunctive/less potent) are all acromegaly therapies; mixed surgical/drug tiles are intentional. Ref: Katznelson L et al. JCEM 2014.

Connection Title: Drugs that reduce peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion
Explanation: The source lists PTU, beta blockers, glucocorticoids and amiodarone as inhibitors of peripheral thyroid hormone conversion. Propranolol is the beta blocker named elsewhere in the thyroid section.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Peripheral deiodination inhibitors; Drugs inhibiting T4 activation
Source Section: T3, T4 Synthesis and Pharmacology, p. 25; Graves Disease: Management, p. 26
Notes: Confirmed inhibitors of peripheral T4-to-T3 (type I 5'-deiodinase): PTU, glucocorticoids, amiodarone, and propranolol. QUALIFIER: propranolol inhibits conversion only at high dose (>160 mg/day) and the effect is not clinically relevant at usual doses; do not generalize to all beta-blockers. Ref: Burch HB. Drug Effects on the Thyroid. NEJM 2019; Van Uytfanghe K et al. Thyroid 2023; FDA levothyroxine label.

Connection Title: Components of the source thyroid-storm regimen
Explanation: The source four-part regimen combines adrenergic control, a thionamide, a glucocorticoid and iodine. This is a regimen association, not a shared mechanism.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Four Ps of thyroid storm; Source-listed thyroid storm therapies
Notes: ATA-supported thyroid-storm regimen: thionamide (PTU) + beta-blocker (propranolol) + glucocorticoid + iodide (KI). CRITICAL QUALIFIER: iodide must be given >=1 h AFTER the thionamide; not simultaneous or a universally required set. ATA names hydrocortisone or dexamethasone as the glucocorticoid, so 'prednisolone' is a defensible but non-canonical substitute. Ref: Ross DS et al. ATA 2016 Hyperthyroidism Guidelines, Thyroid; Wiersinga WM et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2023.

Connection Title: Characteristic associations of Graves disease
Explanation: Receptor-stimulating antibodies increase thyroid activity; orbital and pretibial tissue changes and diffuse gland uptake are characteristic Graves associations.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Graves disease clues; Autoimmune hyperthyroidism
Notes: TSI (TRAb), exophthalmos, pretibial myxedema, and diffuse increased RAIU are characteristic of Graves; orbitopathy/dermopathy are not present in every patient (association wording correct). Ref: Lee SY, Pearce EN. Hyperthyroidism: A Review. JAMA 2023.

Connection Title: Antibody and histology clues to Hashimoto thyroiditis
Explanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis is associated with thyroid autoantibodies, oncocytic follicular-cell changes and lymphoid aggregates with germinal centers.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hashimoto thyroiditis findings; Chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis
Notes: Anti-TPO, anti-Tg, Hurthle (oncocytic) cells, and germinal-center lymphoid follicles are characteristic of Hashimoto; none is individually specific, so 'autoimmune thyroiditis' is acceptable only with a compatible explanation. Ref: Robbins & Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease 10e.

Connection Title: Clues to subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
Explanation: De Quervain thyroiditis classically follows a viral-like illness, causes thyroid pain and inflammatory-marker elevation, and shows granulomatous inflammation with giant cells.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: De Quervain thyroiditis; Subacute painful thyroiditis
Notes: Painful tender thyroid, antecedent viral-like illness, elevated ESR, and granulomatous giant cells define subacute (De Quervain) thyroiditis; the preceding illness is an association, not proof of a specific virus. Ref: Robbins & Cotran 10e.

Connection Title: Classic findings in congenital hypothyroidism
Explanation: Congenital thyroid hormone deficiency can produce an enlarged protruding tongue, a protruding umbilicus, a hoarse cry and reduced muscle tone.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Congenital thyroid hormone deficiency; Neonatal hypothyroidism clues
Notes: Macroglossia, umbilical protrusion/hernia, hoarse cry, and hypotonia are classic congenital hypothyroidism findings; individually nonspecific and 'can produce' wording preserved. Ref: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 21e.

Connection Title: Molecular and microscopic clues to papillary thyroid carcinoma
Explanation: Papillary thyroid carcinoma is associated with characteristic nuclear clearing, calcified psammoma bodies and the listed oncogenic alterations.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Papillary thyroid cancer associations; Papillary carcinoma clues
Notes: Orphan-Annie-eye nuclei, psammoma bodies, BRAF V600E, and RET/PTC rearrangements characterize PTC; BRAF and RET/PTC are mutually exclusive drivers (not coexisting), and somatic RET/PTC differs from the germline RET of MEN2. Ref: Fagin JA, Wells SA. NEJM 2016; Boucai L et al. Thyroid Cancer. JAMA 2024; Adeniran AJ et al. Am J Surg Pathol 2006.

Connection Title: Associations of follicular thyroid carcinoma
Explanation: Follicular carcinoma is distinguished from adenoma by capsular and/or vascular invasion, commonly spreads through blood and can harbor a PAX8-PPAR-gamma fusion.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Follicular thyroid cancer; Follicular carcinoma associations
Notes: Capsular invasion, vascular invasion, hematogenous spread, and PAX8-PPAR-gamma fusion characterize follicular carcinoma; capsular/vascular invasion are alternatives distinguishing it from adenoma (not both required) and the fusion is not universal. Ref: Boucai L et al. JAMA 2024; Dettmer MS. Virchows Arch 2026.

Connection Title: Associations of medullary thyroid carcinoma
Explanation: Medullary carcinoma arises from C cells, produces calcitonin, can deposit stromal amyloid and is associated with RET alterations, including hereditary MEN2 disease.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Medullary thyroid cancer; C-cell carcinoma associations
Notes: C-cell (parafollicular) origin, calcitonin, amyloid stroma, and RET; RET is not present in every sporadic tumor, so MEN2 should not be inferred from all cases. Ref: Boucai L et al. JAMA 2024; Neumann HPH et al. NEJM 2019.

Connection Title: Manifestations of hypocalcemic neuromuscular excitability
Explanation: Low calcium can increase neuromuscular excitability, producing the two bedside signs, tetany and seizures.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Hypocalcemia findings; Low-calcium excitability
Notes: Chvostek, Trousseau, tetany, and seizures reflect hypocalcemic neuromuscular excitability; nonspecific and not universally present, and tetany overlaps mechanistically with the elicited signs. Hypoparathyroidism is one cause, not the only diagnosis. Ref: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 14e.

Connection Title: Classic clinical consequences of hypercalcemia
Explanation: The source associates elevated calcium with stone disease, slowed intestinal transit, skeletal pain and psychiatric or cognitive symptoms.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Stones bones groans and psychiatric overtones; Hypercalcemia symptoms
Source Section: Parathyroid Location and Function, p. 35; Hyperparathyroidism, p. 38
Notes: Nephrolithiasis, constipation, bone pain, and neuropsychiatric symptoms are classic hypercalcemia manifestations (severity/chronicity-dependent). Ambiguity reassessed from 2 to 1: 'primary hyperparathyroidism' is a cause of the same hypercalcemia, effectively an alternate label rather than a competing category. BOARD OVERLAP WARNING: do not co-place a separate hyperparathyroidism-symptom connection. Ref: Walker MD, Shane E. Hypercalcemia: A Review. JAMA 2022.

Connection Title: Calcium-raising and phosphate-lowering actions of PTH
Explanation: PTH conserves renal calcium, promotes phosphaturia, stimulates calcitriol formation and indirectly increases osteoclast-mediated resorption through osteoblast-lineage cells.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: PTH actions; Parathyroid hormone effects
Notes: Distal tubular Ca reabsorption, phosphaturia, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase induction, and (indirect, RANKL-mediated via osteoblast-lineage cells) osteoclastic resorption are core PTH actions; resorption assumes sustained PTH signaling and is not direct on osteoclasts. Ref: Walker MD, Silverberg SJ. Nat Rev Endocrinol 2018; Guyton & Hall 14e.

Connection Title: Malabsorptive settings that predispose to vitamin D deficiency
Explanation: The source lists these settings as causes of impaired vitamin D absorption and deficiency. Risk depends on disease severity, anatomy and treatment.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Malabsorption-associated vitamin D deficiency; Reduced vitamin D absorption
Notes: Celiac, cystic fibrosis, IBD, and gastric bypass impair absorption of fat-soluble vitamin D; malabsorption is not universal in all IBD or after every bypass, so 'predispose' wording is appropriate. Ref: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 14e.

Connection Title: Typical laboratory tendencies in primary hyperparathyroidism
Explanation: Autonomous PTH secretion can raise calcium, promote phosphate loss and increase bone turnover with alkaline phosphatase elevation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Primary hyperparathyroidism laboratory profile; PTH-driven hypercalcemia
Notes: High Ca, high or inappropriately-normal PTH, and low phosphate are typical of primary HPT; ALP is often NORMAL in mild disease and PTH may be inappropriately normal rather than frankly elevated - this is a 'typical profile', not diagnostic criteria. Ref: Walker MD, Silverberg SJ. Nat Rev Endocrinol 2018; Bilezikian JP et al. Lancet 2018; Insogna KL. NEJM 2018.

Connection Title: Laboratory pattern of CKD-related secondary hyperparathyroidism
Explanation: Impaired renal phosphate excretion and calcitriol generation can lower calcium and stimulate secondary PTH secretion in CKD.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Renal secondary hyperparathyroidism; CKD mineral metabolism changes
Notes: Phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol drive low/low-normal Ca and elevated PTH in CKD; values vary with CKD stage and therapy, so the low-normal calcium qualifier avoids making hypocalcemia universal. Ref: KDIGO 2017 CKD-MBD Guideline; Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 14e.

Connection Title: Clues to familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
Explanation: The source CaSR-associated form shifts calcium sensing in the parathyroids and kidneys, causing inherited hypercalcemia with relatively low urinary calcium.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: FHH; Inherited hypocalciuric hypercalcemia
Notes: Inactivating CaSR variant, autosomal dominant inheritance, hypercalcemia with inappropriately low urinary calcium (Ca:Cr clearance ratio <0.01); not every molecular subtype involves CaSR. Ref: Bilezikian JP et al. Lancet 2018; Wilhelm SM et al. AAES Guidelines, JAMA Surg 2016.

Connection Title: Laboratory clues to untreated primary adrenal insufficiency
Explanation: Adrenal failure lowers cortisol and mineralocorticoid output. Loss of cortisol feedback raises ACTH; mineralocorticoid deficiency can impair potassium excretion.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Addison disease laboratory clues; Primary adrenal failure
Notes: High ACTH, low cortisol, low aldosterone, and hyperkalemia characterize untreated primary AI; hyperkalemia is present in only ~50% at diagnosis, and preserved aldosterone distinguishes secondary/tertiary AI. Ref: Vaidya A et al. Adrenal Insufficiency. JAMA 2025; Husebye ES et al. J Intern Med 2014; Bornstein SR et al. Endocrine Society 2016.

Connection Title: Characteristic physical findings of Cushing syndrome
Explanation: Excess glucocorticoid effect produces skin and connective-tissue changes and altered fat distribution, including these findings.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Cushingoid appearance; Physical findings of glucocorticoid excess
Notes: Purple striae, thin skin, central adiposity, and dorsocervical fat pad reflect glucocorticoid excess and also fit chronic exogenous steroid effect; do not label 'Cushing disease' (pituitary-source-specific). Ref: Nieman LK et al. Endocrine Society Cushing Guideline, JCEM 2008.

Connection Title: Causes of renin-driven secondary hyperaldosteronism
Explanation: Reduced effective renal perfusion in heart or liver failure, renal artery narrowing and a renin-secreting tumor can activate renin-mediated aldosterone production.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: High-renin hyperaldosteronism; Secondary aldosterone excess
Notes: CHF, cirrhosis/liver failure, renal artery stenosis, and reninoma cause renin-driven (secondary) hyperaldosteronism via reduced effective renal perfusion or autonomous renin secretion; liver-failure link depends on effective arterial underfilling. 'Increased renin' is an accepted mechanism-based alternate category. Ref: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 14e.

Connection Title: Hereditary syndromes associated with pheochromocytoma
Explanation: The source lists all four syndromes as hereditary associations of pheochromocytoma, an adrenal chromaffin-cell tumor.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Inherited pheochromocytoma predisposition; Familial pheochromocytoma syndromes
Notes: NF1, VHL, MEN2A, and MEN2B are established hereditary pheochromocytoma predisposition syndromes; penetrance varies (pheo ~50% in MEN2, 10-20% in VHL, ~2% in NF1) and pheo is not inevitable. MEN2A/2B share RET biology but remain distinct. Ref: Neumann HPH et al. NEJM 2019; Taieb D et al. EANM/SNMMI 2019.

Connection Title: Molecular and diagnostic associations of neuroblastoma
Explanation: Neuroblastoma can show MYCN amplification, increased catecholamine metabolites in urine and neuroblastic rosettes on microscopy.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Neuroblastoma clues; Neuroblastoma tumor associations
Notes: MYCN amplification (prognostic subset, not universal), urinary VMA and HVA (distinct catecholamine metabolites), and Homer-Wright rosettes characterize neuroblastoma; rosettes also occur in other neural tumors. Ref: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics 21e; Robbins & Cotran 10e.

Connection Title: Recessive enzyme defects affecting sex-steroid synthesis or activation
Explanation: The source groups these inherited enzyme defects when evaluating differences in sex development and describes each as autosomal recessive. They affect androgen synthesis or androgen activation.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Autosomal recessive steroid enzyme deficiencies; Recessive defects of androgen synthesis or activation
Source Section: Adrenal Cortex Pathways Overview and Enzyme Deficiencies, pp. 51-56
Notes: All four are autosomal recessive enzyme deficiencies of sex-steroid synthesis (21-OH, 17-alpha-OH, 11-beta-OH) or androgen activation (5-alpha-reductase). CRITICAL: 5-alpha-reductase deficiency is NOT a form of CAH - never accept an 'all are CAH' label. Shared autosomal recessive inheritance is the clean unifying category. Ref: El-Maouche D et al. CAH, Lancet 2017; Thigpen AE et al. NEJM 1992; MedlinePlus '5-alpha reductase deficiency'.

Connection Title: Laboratory clues to salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Explanation: Blocked steroid synthesis raises 17-hydroxyprogesterone. In the classic salt-wasting form, mineralocorticoid deficiency causes sodium loss, increased renin and impaired potassium excretion.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia; Classic salt-wasting CYP21A2 deficiency
Notes: Elevated 17-OHP with mineralocorticoid deficiency (elevated renin, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia) defines classic salt-wasting 21-OH deficiency; do not generalize the electrolyte pattern to non-classic or simple-virilizing forms. Ref: El-Maouche D et al. Lancet 2017 (Table 2).

Connection Title: Steroid and electrolyte pattern of 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency
Explanation: Impaired 17-alpha-hydroxylation reduces sex-steroid synthesis while increasing mineralocorticoid-active precursors, producing hypertension and potassium loss.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: CYP17A1 deficiency pattern; Mineralocorticoid excess with deficient sex steroids
Notes: 17-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP17A1) deficiency: elevated DOC/corticosterone -> hypertension + hypokalemia with REDUCED androgens/sex steroids; low androgens is the discriminator from 11-beta-OH deficiency. BOARD OVERLAP: shares 3 tiles with ENDO-034 - do not co-place in one board. Ref: El-Maouche D et al. Lancet 2017; Willemsen AL et al. JCEM 2025; Stolting G et al. Nat Rev Nephrol 2026.

Connection Title: Steroid and electrolyte pattern of 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency
Explanation: Impaired 11-beta-hydroxylation accumulates a mineralocorticoid-active precursor and increases androgen production, causing hypertension with possible potassium loss and virilization.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: CYP11B1 deficiency pattern; Hypertensive virilizing CAH
Notes: 11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) deficiency: accumulated DOC (mineralocorticoid) -> hypertension + hypokalemia with ELEVATED androgens (virilizing); HTN/hypokalemia are not present in every age group/case. BOARD OVERLAP: shares 3 tiles with ENDO-033 - do not co-place. Ref: El-Maouche D et al. Lancet 2017; Stolting G et al. Nat Rev Nephrol 2026.

Connection Title: Clues to 5-alpha-reductase deficiency in a 46,XY patient
Explanation: Reduced conversion of testosterone to DHT impairs DHT-dependent external development while preserving testosterone-dependent internal structures. Pubertal testosterone increases can cause virilization.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Impaired DHT formation; 5-alpha-reductase deficiency
Notes: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency (46,XY): reduced DHT, elevated T:DHT ratio, preserved testosterone-dependent Wolffian internal structures, pubertal virilization; the 46,XY qualifier is essential and 'internal structures' means T-dependent male ducts. Ref: Thigpen AE et al. NEJM 1992; Reyes AP et al. Nat Rev Urol 2023; MedlinePlus.

Connection Title: Actions enhanced by insulin signaling
Explanation: Insulin promotes anabolic metabolism and brings GLUT4 to the surface of responsive skeletal muscle and adipose cells, increasing glucose uptake.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Anabolic insulin actions; Effects of insulin signaling
Source Section: Insulin Physiology, p. 62; Diabetes Mellitus, p. 63; Type 1 Management, p. 67
Notes: Insulin promotes glycogenesis, lipogenesis, and protein synthesis (anabolic) and GLUT4 translocation (a trafficking event) in muscle/adipose; GLUT4 is not the insulin-responsive transporter in all tissues, so the 'signaling' title framing is appropriate. Ref: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology 14e.

Connection Title: Organ-specific autoimmune diseases that cluster together (autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 spectrum)
Explanation: All four are organ-specific autoimmune diseases that co-cluster through shared HLA class II haplotypes (DR3-DQ2/DR4-DQ8). Autoimmune adrenal insufficiency, autoimmune thyroid disease, and type 1 diabetes define autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 (Schmidt syndrome); celiac disease is a frequently associated condition.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 spectrum; Polyautoimmunity associated with type 1 diabetes
Source Section: Diabetes Mellitus Type 1, p. 63; Primary Adrenal Insufficiency, p. 44
Notes: REVISED: original title ('...linked to type 1 diabetes') made type 1 diabetes a tile in a category defined by itself (circular). Retitled to an autoimmune-cluster framing in which all four are members. Celiac is an associated condition, not a defining APS-2 criterion; do not assign one specific APS subtype to every combination. Added refs beyond source: Husebye ES et al. Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndromes. NEJM 2018; Grasso EA, Chiarelli F. Pediatr Diabetes 2022.

Connection Title: Renal pathologic findings of diabetic nephropathy
Explanation: Chronic diabetic injury can thicken the glomerular basement membrane, scar glomeruli and produce hyaline deposition in both afferent and efferent arterioles.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Diabetic nephropathy pathology; Diabetic renal microvascular injury
Notes: GBM thickening, (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodular) glomerulosclerosis, and hyalinosis of BOTH afferent and efferent arterioles characterize diabetic nephropathy; efferent arteriolar involvement helps distinguish it from hypertensive nephrosclerosis (afferent-predominant). Not all lesions in every patient. Ref: Robbins & Cotran 10e.

Connection Title: Precipitants shared by DKA and HHS
Explanation: The source lists infection, lack of diabetes medication, MI and pancreatitis as triggers of both hyperglycemic crises. The insulin-omission tile refers to patients prescribed insulin.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Triggers of hyperglycemic crises; DKA and HHS precipitants
Source Section: Diabetic Ketoacidosis, p. 65; Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State, p. 66
Notes: Infection, insulin omission (in insulin-treated patients), MI, and pancreatitis precipitate both DKA and HHS; source 'lack of medication' rendered as insulin omission. Ref: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes; Umpierrez G, Korytkowski M. Nat Rev Endocrinol 2016.

Connection Title: Classic clues to diabetic ketoacidosis
Explanation: Insulin deficiency promotes ketone formation. Acid accumulation produces an anion gap acidosis with compensatory deep breathing; acetone contributes to fruity breath.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: DKA findings; Diabetic ketotic acidosis
Source Section: Diabetic Ketoacidosis: Pathophysiology and Presentation, p. 65
Notes: Kussmaul respirations, fruity (acetone) breath, ketonemia, and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis are classic DKA; other ketoacidoses can mimic, so include diabetes context if those appear on a board. Not all findings in every case. Ref: ADA Standards of Care; Robbins & Cotran 10e.

Connection Title: Sulfonylureas that stimulate insulin release via KATP-channel closure
Explanation: These sulfonylureas close beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels, causing depolarization and calcium-dependent insulin secretion.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Sulfonylureas; Beta-cell KATP-channel closing sulfonylureas
Notes: Tolbutamide (1st-generation), glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride (2nd-generation) are sulfonylureas that close beta-cell K-ATP channels -> depolarization and insulin secretion; do not label 'all second-generation'. 'Sulfonylureas' is an accepted class-based alternate. Ref: Katzung Basic & Clinical Pharmacology 15e.

Connection Title: Source-listed glucose-lowering agents associated with weight loss
Explanation: The source associates metformin, SGLT2 inhibition and the two named GLP1 agonists with weight loss. These effects differ in magnitude and are not guaranteed.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Diabetes medications associated with weight loss; Weight-reducing antihyperglycemic drugs
Notes: Metformin (weight-neutral to modest ~2-3% loss), SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin), and GLP-1 agonists (exenatide, liraglutide) are associated with weight loss; magnitude GLP-1 > SGLT2 > metformin. 'Associated with', not guaranteed; metformin may be weight-neutral. Ref: Davies MJ et al. ADA/EASD 2022, Diabetologia; Tsapas A et al. Diabetes Obes Metab 2021 (network meta-analysis).
